title: Verstappen thrilled with first Singapore win at 10th attempt
excerpt:
Max Verstappen expressed his pride and satisfaction after claiming a long-awaited Singapore Grand Prix win – the result coming in the Dutchman’s 10th attempt.

Verstappen had scored four podium finishes around the Marina Bay Street Circuit in previous years, including back-to-back P2 results in 2024 and 2025, but victory eluded him.

That was until this weekend, where he proved to be the class of the field across the Sprint and main Grand Prix, with P1 on Sunday night meaning from the current F1 calendar, he has only yet to win at the new-for-2026 Madring.

Speaking after the triumph, which also came during his 250th Grand Prix start, Verstappen smiled: “It’s taken a while, but I think this race was very good.

“We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre and on the medium, even though I think the medium tyre for everyone was a bit more of a struggle.

“It worked out, so of course I’m very happy to win here.”

Verstappen set up his drive to victory with a stern defence against Ferrari rival Charles Leclerc at the start, admitting that his getaway was “just good enough”, before building and controlling an advantage at the head of the field.

It also gives Verstappen and Red Bull successive wins, following their breakthrough first victory of the 2026 season last time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Reflecting on the recent upturn, which came after significant updates in Azerbaijan, Verstappen added: “I think the last few races have been really positive for us, and it’s just great to see. We have a lot of motivation in the team to try and deliver even more results.

“It’s a really good group of people. I really enjoy working with them, and hopefully we can have a bit more fun until the end of the year.”

title: Verstappen seals commanding Singapore victory
excerpt:
Max Verstappen put in an assured drive to take victory in the Singapore Grand Prix, the Red Bull driver holding the lead throughout the hot and humid encounter to seal his first-ever Grand Prix win at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

After defending against Charles Leclerc into the first corner, Verstappen ensured that he emerged in P1 and, while the Ferrari initially remained on his tail, the four-time World Champion soon built up a significant gap at the front.

The mid-race pit stops phase did little to change Verstappen’s commanding run, the Dutchman enjoying a smooth stop as he switched from the soft to the medium tyres.

From there onwards he was untroubled at the front and, despite suffering some radio issues that resulted in the team having to use the pit board for communication, Verstappen ultimately clinched his 73rd career win on his 250th Grand Prix start.

Leclerc held onto P2, crossing the line 7.3 seconds behind, while Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli completed the podium in third – a result that would extend the youngster’s championship lead further.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were fourth and fifth, ahead of the other Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton. Liam Lawson claimed P7 to add to Racing Bulls’ tally, with Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg just behind in eighth.

Mercedes’ George Russell and Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar put in good recovery drives from the back of the field and the pit lane respectively, the pair rounding out the top 10 to claim P9 and P10 respectively.

Pierre Gasly just missed out for Alpine in 11th, ahead of the Haas duo of Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon, Williams’ Carlos Sainz and Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad.

Fernando Alonso brought his Aston Martin home in P16, followed by Cadillac’s Sergio Perez. Alex Albon was classified as P18 for Williams despite retiring in the closing stages, while the other Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas rounded out the order in P19.

Three drivers retired from the event, with Aston Martin’s Lance Stroll suffering a suspected clutch issue, Alpine’s Franco Colapinto experiencing a driveline problem and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto experiencing what appeared to be a gearbox problem.

AS IT HAPPENED

The first two days on track at the Marina Bay Street Circuit had already proven to be action-packed, with Verstappen emerging as the winner of a dramatic, rain-affected Sprint before securing pole position – his first at this venue – a few hours later in Qualifying.

But now it was time for the main event, as the attentions of the paddock turned to the 62-lap Singapore Grand Prix. Hot and humid conditions were again in force as the drivers started their preparations for the event, while some would perhaps breathe a sigh of relief that no further rain had arrived as of yet.

It was confirmed in the build-up to the race that a few alterations had been made to the starting order, with Russell dropping back to P19 due to an engine penalty. Hadjar, meanwhile, was set to line up from the pit lane following the use of additional power unit elements, the Frenchman having been eliminated in Q1 of Qualifying after troubles with his car.

Hadjar would not be alone in starting from the pit lane, as the Aston Martin pair of Alonso and Stroll were also facing the same fate – the former’s car having taken on a new power unit component, while the latter’s had been modified under Parc Ferme conditions.

There looked to be a problem on Antonelli’s Mercedes en route to the grid, with the mechanics seen working on the brakes when the car had lined up in its P4 slot. This appeared resolved as lights-out neared – but would it impact the championship leader in the race?

When all 22 cars were in place under the floodlights and the tyres blankets had been removed, it was revealed that the grid were evenly split in terms of those starting on the soft and medium compounds for the expected one-stop encounter. Polesitter Verstappen was amongst those on the soft, while third-placed Hamilton had opted for the medium tyre.

Once the formation lap had been completed, the five lights went out to get the Singapore Grand Prix underway – and after a good start from Leclerc in P2, Verstappen cut across to ensure that he held the lead ahead of the Monegasque into the first corner.

While Norris and Piastri ran close to one another, the pair managed to avoid a repeat of their Sprint collision before Norris then turned his attentions to chasing after Antonelli in fourth. Elsewhere Lawson had gained a position to move into P7, while Hulkenberg and Sainz had also made their way into the top 10 in eighth and 10th respectively.

Further back, the Haas duo of Ocon and Bearman engaged in an intra-team scrap over P11, resulting in Bearman ultimately coming out ahead. Russell, meanwhile, had worked his way up to 15th place by Lap 5 following his start from the back of the grid.

Leclerc was keeping Verstappen honest at the front, the Ferrari running only 0.6s behind – allowing him to have Overtake Mode. The gap opened up again as Lap 7 got underway, however, with the battle looking likely to ebb and flow.

The Virtual Safety Car was deployed when Bortoleto pulled off track towards the pit lane exit, the Audi seemingly experiencing a gearbox issue. Once the car had been pushed back into the pit lane and towards the team’s garage, the VSC period came to an end.

There was further drama when Bortoleto’s stricken car caught fire, with the marshals extinguishing the flames while the pit lane entry was briefly closed. Meanwhile Sainz had been noted for leaving the track and gaining an advantage – the Spaniard having sparked the ire of Lindblad with a move on the first lap – but it was later deemed that no further investigation was necessary.

More than 10 laps down, Verstappen remained 0.8s clear of Leclerc while Hamilton had dropped back slightly on the medium tyres. The seven-time World Champion was being closely followed by Antonelli, with the McLarens of Norris and Piastri also not far behind.

“I think Plan C and opposite to Red Bull,” Leclerc radioed in. There was also strategy talk going on for Norris, the Briton’s race engineer asking if he still felt that his idea from an earlier meeting “would be best” – to which Norris responded that he did.

Over at Red Bull, Verstappen was told: “If we can continue to eke this out, it will only help our cause.” The Dutch driver’s lead now stood at 2.6s by Lap 15, while team mate Hadjar had recovered to P16. Russell’s journey up the order also appeared to be going well, with the Mercedes driver in 12th and rapidly catching the Haas pair.

The strategy discussions were ongoing across the field, with Hamilton informed that he would need to “pick up the pace” for “Plan C”. After responding that he did not have any more, the Briton was told that “Plan B” might be the better option. Would that see Hamilton embark on a two-stop strategy?

On Lap 19 the Ferrari crew emerged from the pit lane – and it was indeed for Hamilton, who returned to the track in P7 on fresh soft tyres behind the Racing Bulls machine of Lawson. Elsewhere Norris felt that Antonelli ahead had exceeded track limits, an offence that the Italian has committed more than once during the season so far.

It did not take long for Hamilton to gain a place, having picked off Lawson for P6 on Lap 21. The Ferrari racer remained the only driver to have made a pit stop – but Leclerc warned over the radio that his own tyres could not last much longer.

Antonelli was informed that he had indeed exceeded track limits twice at Turn 2. Further back, the other Mercedes of Russell had another car in his sights as he closed in further on Ocon in 11th – and the Briton ultimately swept down the inside of the Haas into Turn 16 to seal the position.

The pit lane became busy again on Lap 24 when Antonelli pitted for the medium tyres – bringing him back out in sixth behind Hamilton – before Leclerc also dived into the pit lane one tour later, re-emerging just a fraction in front of his team mate in fourth. With Hamilton seemingly quicker on the soft rubber, would the team think about swapping the two cars?

“We lost two seconds that last lap,” Hamilton reported as he remained stuck behind the other Ferrari, amid question marks over whether the World Champion would embark on a two-stop strategy or hold out on his current tyres for a one-stop. Leclerc, meanwhile, pumped in a new fastest lap.

With Leclerc, Hamilton and Antonelli the only drivers to pit from the top 10, Verstappen held a 17.9s lead by Lap 28 over Norris while Piastri followed in third. Further back, Lawson was in a somewhat lonely seventh, ahead of Hulkenberg, Gasly and Bearman.

That order changed when Gasly pitted on Lap 30 – but there was trouble for his team mate on the next tour, with Colapinto having pulled off track with a suspected driveline issue. Hulkenberg was the next to pit and returned in P10, handing another position to Russell as the Briton continued his ascent in ninth.

“I feel something leaking between my feet,” Antonelli reported over the radio, while Verstappen headed into the pits on Lap 33 for a set of medium tyres and retained his lead in the process. Norris also made his stop shortly afterwards and re-emerged in sixth behind Antonelli.

Next to pit was Piastri, with the Australian experiencing a slightly slow stop as he returned to the track in P6, six seconds behind his team mate. With others also visiting the pits, Russell – in P7 – was now the only driver in the top 10 yet to make a stop.

“Charles is trying to pick up the pace – he is on Plan C, we are on Plan B,” Hamilton was informed on Lap 37, with the British driver now running 2.4s behind the other red car, while just behind Antonelli had been shown a black and white flag for track limits.

The Italian asked Race Engineer Pete ‘Bono’ Bonnington to check the car after feeling some “weird behaviour”, before being reassured that there appeared to be “no concern” from the team’s side.

The yellow flags were thrown when Stroll’s Aston Martin came to a halt at Turn 15 due to a clutch issue, with a Virtual Safety Car subsequently being deployed. Leclerc and Antonelli both headed into the pits for a second stop – but Russell dived in for his first just as the VSC was ending, meaning that the Mercedes driver could not quite benefit to the same extent.

This brought him out into P10, while Leclerc was in third – now some 10 seconds behind Hamilton – and Antonelli separated the McLarens in P5. But the championship leader did not seem happy, going on to report struggles with his brakes.

Piastri made a second pit stop on Lap 42, the Australian having suffered a slow puncture as he returned to the track in sixth. Antonelli, meanwhile, was told that “heat soak” had caused the fluid around his feet, while the team also reminded the Italian to remain cautious of track limits.

Debate appeared to be continuing at Ferrari over Hamilton’s strategy, with the team seemingly believing that he was a few laps short of making it to the end on his tyres. On Lap 46 the Briton was overtaken by Leclerc, the Monegasque showing better pace on his fresher rubber – but he remained 15 seconds adrift of Verstappen in the lead.

Russell was looking racy, meanwhile, as he tried to find a way past Gasly for P9, the Silver Arrows driver eventually making the move into Turn 7 on Lap 48 – but there was less positive news for the other Mercedes of Antonelli, the championship leader seemingly at risk of a penalty after exceeding track limits again.

As Lap 52 ticked down – with 10 laps remaining – Verstappen continued to lead by just under 10 seconds from Leclerc, with Hamilton some 11.8s adrift of his team mate in third. Norris, meanwhile, had closed to within half a second of Hamilton, followed by Antonelli, Piastri, Lawson, Hulkenberg, Russell and Gasly.

Verstappen looked to be having issues with his radio, with Race Engineer Gianpiero ‘GP’ Lambiase struggling to hear the Dutchman when asking for his thoughts on whether he would want to pit again in the event of another Safety Car.

The fight for the final spot on the podium was heating up, with Hamilton going wide as he tried to defend against Norris – before Antonelli took advantage to sweep ahead of the McLaren and close in on Hamilton. A few moments later the Italian had snatched P3 into Turn 16, while Hamilton found himself under investigation for leaving the track and gaining an advantage. It was subsequently decided that no further action was required.

As Hamilton continued to struggle on his tyres, Norris soon overtook to snatch fourth place from the Briton. Elsewhere Russell appeared stuck behind Hulkenberg in the battle for eighth, while Norris was struggling to stay with Antonelli and asked if any help would be possible behind – just as Piastri was continuing to chase down Hamilton.

Norris – after being warned of a ”developing potential sensor issue” – asked if he could help Piastri, the Australian now all over the back of Hamilton in the scrap for fifth. After a few tries, Piastri ultimately made his move into Turn 16 to take the position.

Up ahead, Verstappen took the chequered flag to seal a commanding Grand Prix victory – the first time he has done so at the Marina Bay Street Circuit – while Leclerc and Antonelli completed the podium and Norris and Piastri brought home fourth and fifth for McLaren.

Hamilton had to settle for sixth, and the Briton issued an apology to his team over the radio – seemingly suggesting that the decision not to pit for a second time had been his. Behind him the top 10 was completed by Lawson, Hulkenberg, Russell and Hadjar.

Gasly, Bearman, Ocon, Sainz, Lindblad, Alonso and Perez were next in the classification, with Albon retiring but placing in P18 while Bottas was the final name in the order, following the earlier retirements of Stroll, Colapinto and Bortoleto.

Key quote

"It’s taken a while, but I think this race was very good," said Verstappen. "We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre and on the medium, even though I think the medium tyre for everyone was a bit more of a struggle. It worked out, so of course I’m very happy to win here."

What's next

title: Racing Bulls to make driver decision 'in the coming weeks'
excerpt:
Racing Bulls will settle on their driver line-up for the 2027 season “in the coming weeks” according to Team Principal Alan Permane, who is still working to decide between three major contenders.

Every team except Racing Bulls and Haas have announced that they will stick with their current pairings heading into next year, bringing greater focus onto whether the Faenza-based outfit will offer new deals to Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad.

Both drivers have made the most of the team’s pace to regularly finish in the points and take Racing Bulls to P5 in the constructors’ standings, with Lawson scoring a total of 69 points – 14 of which came from his stint as Isack Hadjar’s substitute at Red Bull – while rookie Lindblad has netted 38 so far.

However, it’s no secret that Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov is waiting in the wings for an opportunity to race in Formula 1, having impressed by competing for the Formula 2 title in his first full season.

Asked ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix when a decision will be made, Permane said: “I don't want to give you a definite date. You know, no, that's not going to work. It's going to be in the coming weeks, let's say.

“I mean, we're in no rush. I think everyone knows we've got two fantastic drivers. We've got a fantastic driver in F2 at the moment, and they're all there and ready to go.

“But three doesn't fit into two, of course, and we're just going to take a little bit more time and make sure we get the right pairing for next year.”

Racing Bulls have acted as a development ground for future Red Bull drivers in the past, with most of the top team’s recent racers proving their skill at the sister team before receiving a promotion.

Permane explained that this responsibility is what complicates the line-up decision as they tend to prioritise giving a chance to juniors, but Lawson and Lindblad are on course to give the squad their best-ever result in the Teams’ Championship.

Elaborating on their driver criteria, Permane said: “There's many, many, many things. I guess top of the list is speed and pace and all that goes with that.

“But there's lots, of course, in the background because we're in a slightly unique situation, I guess. We want to bring on young drivers, we want to bring on young talent, and of course we have one eye on them progressing in the future.

“So, it's not just about the here and now, it's also about what they can do in the future.”

title: What are the tyre strategy options for the Singapore GP?
excerpt:
So, who has the quickest F1 car of 2026? At the moment, it looks very much like Red Bull Racing, with Max Verstappen having an on-song Saturday at Marina Bay, winning the Sprint and taking pole position. After second place in Baku, and victory at Sepang, this triple-header has been the re-emergence of RBR – but can Verstappen seal the deal tomorrow?

The Sprint had plenty of drama, but in and around that, the running order was largely processional. But this isn’t necessarily a good guide to the Grand Prix, where undercuts and tyre deltas play a huge part in determining the outcome, and the final third of the race is usually eventful.

Good strategy can’t necessarily win the Singapore Grand Prix, but strategic errors can certainly lose it. So, what do we have in store on race day?

title: Fred Vasseur bemoans Lewis Hamilton Singapore GP pit call: 'A bit of a shame'
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur believes Lewis Hamilton's poor call cost him a podium in the Singapore Grand Prix.

When a virtual safety car was called on lap 39 for Aston Martin's Lance Stroll retiring with a clutch issue, it opened up a small window of opportunity for a pit stop.

Charles Leclerc took full advantage to switch to another fresh set of tyres, and Hamilton, running three seconds behind, should have followed his team-mate into the pits, only to instead stay out.

It was a decision that backfired for the seven-time F1 champion for although he slotted into second place behind eventual race winner Max Verstappen, on age-old softs that ran for 44 laps, he finished sixth behind Verstappen, Leclerc, Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and McLaren duo Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

At the chequered flag, Hamilton apologised to his team for the decision he made.

"We kept the door open with the two options depending on a VSC, so that was the case," said Vasseur, speaking to Sky Sports F1.

"We called them both to pit, that it would have been P2 and P3, but he missed the pit entry, which is a bit of a shame because he lost a podium."

Vasseur confirmed that another problem for Hamilton was that he started on the medium tyres, opposite to Leclerc on the softs, but with the opportunity on the rubber offset to potentially attack polesitter Verstappen by strategy.

[Article continues below]

Vasseur - We all ran blind

Unfortunately for Hamilton, the yellow-striped compound did not prove as robust as had been hoped, with Hamilton pitting at the end of lap 18 to take on the softs he then ran to the finish.

"The main issue, and it was true for us, true for everybody, that on the grid you are 50-50 [with tyre choice]," said Vasseur. "In FP1 you don't do so many laps, and we all did laps with the hard [tyres] that we didn't touch for the race.

"We were expecting to do the long stint [on the medium] in the sprint, but the sprint race was with intermediate, so we all went into the race completely blind with the tyres.

"Today, the soft was much better than the medium. It's why Lewis struggled at the beginning and a bit less at the end. We were all in the same situation, starting the race a bit blind.

"It's true that for us, with the two cars two and three [on the grid], it was a good opportunity for us to take the fight to Max."

Overall, Vasseur was happy with the weekend after Hamilton and Leclerc finished second and third in the sprint, before the two, six in the grand prix.

"It's a good weekend," said Vasseur. "We did P2 and P3 in the sprint; P2 and P3 in quali; P2 [in the race] and we were not far away from P3.

"Overall, over the weekend, Max was a bit faster than us. We have to try to catch up, but overall, it was a strong performance from the team, from the two drivers, and a good result for us."

title: Lewis Hamilton reveals error over Ferrari disaster in Singapore GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has taken responsibility for the odd Ferrari strategy in the Singapore Grand Prix that left him badly exposed as he fell away to sixth place.

Hamilton started on the medium tyres at Marina Bay, whilst the front-row pair of Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc opted for softs, as Hamilton tried to create some strategic variance to the Red Bull.

In the opening laps, he was able to latch onto both cars ahead, but gradually fell away and became a bottle-neck for those behind, including Kimi Antonelli, Lando Norris, and Oscar Piastri.

With the soft tyres emerging as the favoured race tyre, Hamilton pitted at the end of Lap 18 for his soft tyres, facing either a two-stop strategy or 44 laps on the soft tyres.

He initially cycled to second after a VSC, but Leclerc quickly passed the sister SF-26 after stopping under it, with Hamilton declaring that he wanted to try to go to the end in a bid to save a strong result.

Ultimately, Hamilton's tyres fell off the cliff, and he was passed by Antonelli, Norris, and Piastri in the closing laps as he fell to sixth place in the final results - his equal worst finish of the season, and third time in his last four finishes that he has taken the place following Italy and Azerbaijan, with a third in Sepang and a DNF in Spain.

On the cooldown lap, Hamilton took responsibility for the issue.

"Sorry, boys," Hamilton began.

"I let you down today with that strategy.

"[It was] my call, and I lost us valuable points. I'll try to make up for it in the next one.

"Great job with the pit-stop, though.

Hamilton's engineer Carlo Santi then replied to acknowledge the message.

"Understood, thank you, Lewis."

title: Max Verstappen 'breaks silence' as Red Bull bug plagues stress-free win
excerpt:
Max Verstappen conquered one of the last remaining tracks he had yet to triumph at by winning the Singapore Grand Prix, with just the Madring left to tame.

It was a quiet and sometimes static cruise to victory for Verstappen as the radio issues that plagued him during practice at the Marina Bay Street Circuit returned in an otherwise stress-free win.

Red Bull spent a considerable part of the sole practice session dealing with the bug, and its recurrence led to some creative communication methods between the Dutchman and race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase.

It included Verstappen being asked to open his radio to create the white noise being heard over broadcast or remain silent to indicate strategy preferences.

However, once out of the car, he was keen to focus on the manner of his win, which Jenson Button rightly described as a "masterclass" during the post-race interviews.

"It has taken a while [to win in Singapore], but I think this race was very good," Verstappen said after the chequered flag.

"We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre and on the medium, even though I think the medium for everyone was a bit more of a struggle.

"But it worked out, so very happy to win here."

Back-to-back wins for Verstappen and Red Bull

The victory rubber-stamps Red Bull's return to form, having won on merit last time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the team and Verstappen's first win of the year.

"The last few races have been really positive for us," the four-time F1 drivers' champion added.

"It's just great to see, and we gave a lot of motivation to the team to deliver even more results.

"It's a really good group of people. I really enjoy working with them, and hopefully we can have a bit more fun until the end of the year."

title: Kimi Antonelli caught off-guard by Jenson Button F1 title comment
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli was left stunned after being informed by Jenson Button he could become F1 drivers' champion at the next race in Austin.

Antonelli netted a podium at the end of 62 punishing laps of the Singapore Grand Prix, finishing 17 seconds behind four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

With Mercedes team-mate George Russell rising to ninth, after starting 19th after taking a heavy engine penalty, Antonelli now holds a 102-point cushion over the Briton going into the United States Grand Prix in a fortnight's time.

It means Antonelli could conceivably become champion at the Circuit of the Americas given their are a possible 150 points at stake should F1 go ahead with its plan to race in the final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Button, the 2009 F1 champion, informed Antonelli he could clinch the title at the next race.

There was a look of disbelief on Antonelli's face before he replied: "Can I? Really?", before adding: "Let's not worry about that. Let's try and do the best weekend possible and finish the job."

In what he described as "a very tough race", Antonelli's key moment occurred on lap 54 when he was running fifth directly behind Lewis Hamilton in his Ferrari on age-old soft tyres, and the McLaren of Lando Norris.

At the start of the lap, Norris attempted a move on Hamilton into Turn 1, forcing both to run wide and allowing Antonelli through to steal third.

"Really happy with the podium at the end," said Antonelli. "I managed to take advantage of the fight between Lando and Lewis and make a move on both.

"To bring home P3 is a great result for the team. Yeah, very happy with that."

title: When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' world championship?
excerpt:
When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' championship title?

Following the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix, Kimi Antonelli holds a 102-point lead over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

No other driver is within 100 points of the Italian, who is increasingly set to become the youngest F1 world champion and shatter Sebastian Vettel's record of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days by over three years.

Antonelli, who turned 20 in August 2026, has dominated the season, but when can the Mercedes driver become the first Italian to be crowned world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953?

The article continues below.

THIS ARTICLE WILL BE UPDATED FOLLOWING EVERY GRAND PRIX UNTIL ANTONELLI WINS THE 2026 F1 WORLD DRIVERS' TITLE.

When can Kimi Antonelli win the title?

After the Singapore Grand Prix, there are six races scheduled to take place in the season, each worth 25 points.

This gives a total of 150 points remaining in the championship, with Antonelli holding that 102-point lead after third in Singapore whilst Russell picked up two points for ninth.

A scenario exists whereby Antonelli could win the title in the United States, which is laid out below.

Antonelli wins the United States Grand Prix to extend his points lead to 127. Russell would then be required to finish at least eighth, earning four points to keep the gap to under 125.

Following Austin, 125 points will remain in the season, meaning if he is 125 points or more clear of Russell, he will be champion in the United States, based on countback.

If Antonelli is exactly 125 points ahead of Russell after the Austin race, he would win the title on wins countback, as he would hold eight victories to Russell on three, which could climb to eight over the final five races.

Should Antonelli win the title in the United States, he will be 20 years, 2 months, 1 day old.

title: Max Verstappen lifts Singapore curse with crushing F1 victory
excerpt:
Max Verstappen finally won the Singapore Grand Prix at the 10th attempt with a crushing performance at Marina Bay.

From pole position, Verstappen put in a dominant lights-to-flag victory to record his second successive victory and record his first in the Singapore GP, leaving the new Spanish GP at Madrid as the only circuit on the 2026 calendar he has not won a race at.

Verstappen saw off a strong challenge from Ferrari's Charles Leclerc off the line to lead out of Turn 3 and was relatively untroubled thereafter as he scored a 73rd grand prix victory ahead of Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli finished third, with George Russell in ninth, meaning the gap between the two Mercedes drivers is 102 points. Antonelli now has his first championship point, coming in the United States GP next time out.

Lewis Hamilton suffered a messy strategy race for Ferrari, and finished sixth on a one-stopper as his tyres fell off the cliff in the closing stages.

Verstappen's Singapore dominance

On the grid, a difference in strategy emerged as Verstappen and Leclerc took soft tyres for the start, with Hamilton opting for the mediums to try and create a difference with Verstappen.

At the start, Leclerc tried to slither up the inside of Verstappen, but the Red Bull held firm to keep the lead as Leclerc led Hamilton, Antonelli and the two McLaren drivers of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

Quickly, this leading sextet of cars dropped the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson as Hamilton acted as the cap in the bottle as Verstappen and Leclerc slowly edged away.

Although Leclerc was able to harry Verstappen in the opening laps, by Lap 9, Verstappen had got out of overtake mode activation and pulled away from the Ferrari thereafter, as attention then turned to Hamilton's pace on the mediums.

With the softs proving the best race tyre, Hamilton abandoned his medium strategy on Lap 18 for the switch to softs, and immediately began to set purple laps, and told he was on "Plan C" - a two-stop strategy.

By Lap 24, Leclerc pitted and emerged just ahead of Hamilton for the change to mediums, with this stunting Hamilton's progress.

Verstappen pitted for his change on Lap 32 followed by Norris as it started to become clear that Hamilton's strategy was going to leave him exposed - despite his attempts to ask the team to "tough it out."

At a virtual safety car on Lap 39 for Lance Stroll's stopped Aston Martin, Leclerc and Antonelli both pitted, but Ferrari did not double-stack Hamilton behind the Monegasque, further leaving Hamilton hung out as Leclerc quickly passed him.

Hamilton then fell into the clutches of Norris and Antonelli in the closing laps as he tried to hang on, but as he held Norris up on Lap 54, both drivers went wide at Turn 1, as Antonelli sliced past both in quick succession.

The duelling Hamilton and Norris then allowed Antonelli to escape up the road and wipe out the effects of a potential five-second penalty for track limits - but the move and failure for Russell to get higher than ninth means Antonelli can win the title in the United States.

The gap is now 102 points, with 125 points left after the next race in Austin - meaning if Antonelli wins and Russell does not finish higher than 10th, the Italian will be crowned.

Piastri stole fifth from the struggling Hamilton after a pit-stop just after the VSC for a slow front-right puncture with Lawson hanging onto seventh ahead of Nico Hulkenberg and Russell - who just missed out on being able to pit under the Stroll VSC - and then pitted just as it ended.

Isack Hadjar nabbed the final point from the pit-lane after a late pass on Pierre Gasly.

The non-scorers

The first non-points scorer was Gasly for Alpine, ahead of Oliver Bearman, who enjoyed a clean early battle with team-mate Esteban Ocon, who was 13th.

Carlos Sainz, Arvid Lindblad, Fernando Alonso, Alex Albon, Sergio Perez, and Valtteri Bottas were the other finishers.

There were three drivers who failed to finish the grand prix.

Stroll stopped with a clutch failure, Franco Colapinto of Alpine with a driveline issue, whilst Gabriel Bortoleto suffered an early gearbox failure for Audi.

title: Lando Norris rues missed 'magic' after delicate McLaren balancing act
excerpt:
Lando Norris could not find the "magical" lap he felt was possible during a difficult qualifying session at the Singapore Grand Prix, describing a balancing act so delicate that any deviation from the limit left him "finished".

Norris qualified fifth at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, with McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri down in seventh.

The Australian will, however, start sixth after George Russell's grid penalty, which was triggered by Mercedes exceeding Russell's permitted power unit component allocation.

The session capped a difficult weekend for McLaren, whose MCL40 proved sensitive over Marina Bay's bumps throughout the compressed sprint format.

Norris and Piastri had already endured a costly collision in Saturday's sprint, when Norris attempted a move on his team-mate at Turn 5.

Contact sent both cars into a spin, with Piastri hitting the barriers and retiring on the spot while Norris rejoined to finish eighth. Stewards later ruled it a racing incident, taking no action against either driver.

Reflecting on qualifying, Norris told media, including RacingNews365, that little had changed across the weekend.

"We just are where we have been all weekend; nothing's changed. We're not quick enough," he said.

"There were moments where I would do a good Sector 1 or a good Sector 2, but the car is just so difficult to drive; it's too difficult to drive. We came to a P5 and P7..."

Norris' precarious tightrope walk

The Briton sensed a stronger lap was within reach, but the margin for error proved too narrow to exploit it.

"It felt like there was potential, and it felt like I could maybe put together some magical lap in Q3 if things just went my way," Norris explained.

"But it was just too tricky from a car perspective to be at this limit where if I push 101 per cent, I'm finished. If I push 99 per cent, I'm finished.

"So it's balancing it too much. And on a track like this, with the bumps and everything, it was just too difficult. So no reasons, no excuses. Just not quite good enough."

title: Looming Singapore jeopardy could instigate strategic mayhem for F1 teams
excerpt:
The threat of a safety car or VSC at the Singapore Grand Prix puts what ought to be a comfortable one-stop strategy at risk.

The looming threat of a safety car or virtual safety car at the Singapore Grand Prix could throw F1 teams' race strategies into disarray, with Pirelli outlining the preferred tyre options for Sunday's 62-lap contest.

Marina Bay Street Circuit has produced a safety car in four of the past six grands prix, equating to a 67 per cent probability, while the chance of a virtual safety car stands at 33 per cent over the same period.

That prospect could prove decisive in a race where overtaking is difficult and track position is particularly valuable, potentially forcing teams to reconsider their plans should an early neutralisation present an opportunity for a cheaper pit stop.

Pirelli head of motorsport Dario Marrafuschi expects a one-stop strategy to be the preferred approach under normal racing conditions, with the soft and medium compounds emerging as the strongest combination.

"The severity of the circuit, both in terms of layout, which is mainly a traction and braking circuit, and in terms of roughness, is shifting this event toward the soft side of the tyre choice," Marrafuschi told media, including RacingNews365.

"This was clear since Friday. Actually, it was clear also to all the teams because they started on Friday with a hard set of tyres to make the setup work both on the power units and on the mechanics of the car...

"The hard [tyre] choice is likely something which should not be the main decision for the grid."

Why the one-stop will be king

Marrafuschi outlined the expected pit stop window for the leading strategy, while explaining how an alternative compound could become relevant depending on race circumstances.

"We expect it will be a one-stop race in case of non-authorisation [of the safety car or wet weather protocols], of course... a one-stop race with the soft and medium as the primary choice. Pit stop window opening at Lap 26 out of 62 laps," he said.

"In case you go for a hard choice, maybe for a second stint, the window could open at Lap 23.

"I think the hard choice for the second half of the race may be something that could be considered in case of a safety car in the early laps.

"But also in that case, in my opinion, even though there will be a safety car in the early laps, I think some teams will challenge the medium as well because I think the level of wear will allow teams to do so."

Despite the potential for strategic variation, Pirelli does not expect a conventional two-stop race to be competitive, even if teams opt for the harder compound.

"The last choice for the one-stop is the medium and hard, which overall is five seconds slower than the best one, which is soft and medium," he added.

"And even though it is not recommended, it is still better than a two-stop strategy, which is 10 seconds slower over the race distance. So we don't consider two stops being an option in case of a standard race."

title: Multiple F1 drivers handed pit-lane starts for the Singapore GP
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar, Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll will all start the Singapore Grand Prix from the pit lane.

title: Adjusted Singapore Grand Prix grid after multiple pit lane starts confirmed
excerpt:
2026 F1 Singapore Grand Prix starting grid

George Russell's back-of-the-grid penalty at the Singapore Grand Prix has heavily adjusted the starting line-up at Marina Bay.

Coming into the session, Russell already knew that no matter what he did, he would be starting at the back after Mercedes was forced to take a new power unit for the Briton after his failure in Sepang last time out in the race.

The reason for Hadjar being behind Russell is that the Red Bull suffered gearbox gremlins in Q1 after a power unit change after the Sprint, leaving Hadjar with no time set in qualifying. Thus, under the rules, as he set a time, Russell is ahead of Hadjar.

title: 2026 F1 Singapore Grand Prix - Sunday weather update
excerpt:
F1 faces a potentially more settled evening at the Marina Bay Street Circuit on Sunday, with the threat of rain appearing lower than during a weather-disrupted Saturday at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 62-lap race is scheduled to start at 8pm local time, when temperatures are expected to sit around 27°C, with high humidity making conditions feel warmer for drivers tackling the demanding street circuit.

The latest forecast suggests a relatively low risk of rain during the evening, although showers cannot be entirely ruled out.

Saturday provided a dramatic reminder of Singapore's unpredictable tropical weather. A torrential downpour shortly before the scheduled Sprint start left standing water around the circuit, forcing a 30-minute delay while officials assessed conditions.

Drivers eventually took to the track on intermediate tyres, with heavy spray and changing conditions adding another layer of difficulty to the action.

Friday, by contrast, offered a largely dry start to the weekend, allowing teams to complete their preparations without significant weather disruption.

For Sunday's race, the outlook is more encouraging. Temperatures should remain in the high 20s, with light winds and a relatively modest chance of precipitation through the evening and into the night.

Any passing shower could nevertheless have a significant impact on grip, particularly around the circuit's tight corners and painted street surfaces.

With the race taking place under the floodlights, humidity and heat are likely to remain the principal weather challenges for the drivers.

Teams will also be monitoring radar closely, mindful of Saturday's downpour and the possibility that another tropical shower could change the complexion of the race.

title: Kimi Antonelli reveals narrow Mercedes tightrope in major upgrade question
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has explained how Mercedes now believes it has made a breakthrough with its troubled upgrade introduction, but that the correct window remains "difficult" to find.

For the Singapore weekend, Mercedes has elected to run its car in two different configurations, with Antonelli initially remaining on the new spec car, introduced in Sepang last time out, with George Russell reverted to the old-spec as the team tried to find answers as to why the new parts did not immediately bring a boost to performance.

After a tricky Sprint Qualifying which left him seventh on the grid, going on to finish fourth to open up an 89-point lead over Russell in the championship after the sister car crashed out from the lead, Antonelli qualified fourth for the main race.

Reflecting on the session, the Italian detailed how Mercedes believed it had made a breakthrough with the upgrade - but that finding the right window to extract performance from it remained very small.

"Definitely, we are starting to see what the package can give us. However, it's still difficult to find the right window," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365.

"We did a big step in setup, and we seem to have put the car in a better place, even by giving away a bit of performance. But the car just seemed to work in a better way.

"However, the window was still very small, very sensitive, especially throughout qualifying, but the team did a great job at turning around, and now we start to get some answers. If in Malaysia we were a bit lost, now we have the head a bit clearer.

"[On Friday], the car was just sliding. It was sliding a bit everywhere, so we were just trying to stabilise the car a bit.

"[We gave] away a little bit of aero performance, but having a better, a more stable platform [was key].

"But still, the window, even though it was better to drive, the window was still very small. But I think the good thing is that now we start to see what the package brings and the areas where we need to work on, and we are starting to get some answers, which is a good thing."

title: McLaren lay down seriousness of Lando Norris-Oscar Piastri crash in frank assessment
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has laid down the seriousness with which he is treating the latest on-track collision between Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

In the closing stages of the Sprint race in Singapore, Norris attempted to pass Piastri up the inside of Turn 5, but spun the Australian off and into the barriers whilst the pair were battling over fourth and fifth places.

Piastri was forced out of the Sprint on the spot, with Norris recovering to take eighth place and earn one single - a loss of eight points from the nine it was set to bank through a four-five finish, with the stewards ultimately deciding against taking further action against either driver.

Post-Sprint, Stella and McLaren CEO Zak Brown initially declined to give media interviews, and held talks with both drivers over the breach of the team's papaya rules - which were tested at the Singapore Grand Prix in 2025 when Piastri was furious with Norris's barging past at Turn 3 on the opening lap.

McLaren could have extended its lead over Red Bull to 19 points with a four-five finish and Max Verstappen's victory, but given the eight points Red Bull hauled in, coupled with the one for McLaren, the gap was reduced to 11 with the defending champions on 317 points compared to 306 for the resurgent Red Bull.

Reflecting in his traditional end-of-day media briefing, Stella stressed the seriousness of what Norris and Piastri had done, given the tight battle with Red Bull.

"It is serious because the damage to the team is material," Stella told media, including RacingNews365.

"We are in a close fight in the championship. We had the ambition to challenge Ferrari, and this is a problem in the challenge to the second position. And we have an ambition to finish ahead of Red Bull, and this is a problem to finish ahead of Red Bull.

"It is also serious because we come from a few seasons in which we have reflected together, team and drivers, as to how we approach racing together and how we make sure that the interest of the team is protected.

"It is serious, but at the same time, we approach it with a very constructive mindset, because there's only one outcome: the team will be more united, and the team will be stronger in the way we pursue our quest, which is the drivers' and the team's quests together.

"It is different to say there's any half-full glass here. There isn't at all. The glass is empty because when two McLarens make contact in that way and cause material damage, there's a significant flaw."

McLaren's main beacon

Stella then added that his overriding emotion was one of disappointment but not surprise, but conceded that after a long career in F1, "these things can happen."

"If anything, I am disappointed. Disappointed as a team principal about a situation that is absolutely not acceptable because it caused material damage to the team, and every member of the team knows that the team interest comes before any personal interest," he said.

"But above all, it is the main beacon that guides our action and our instinct. So, not necessarily surprised because I spent so many seasons in Formula 1 and I know that these things can happen.

"But we, as a team, need to reflect on how we make sure that these situations do not happen anymore."
